r31.title: Can we trace each request through the logs?
r31.note: Native request identity and log correlation demonstrated; origin and retry identifiers need an explicit propagation contract.
r31.intro: The requirement is a unique reference for each request, visible in CDN logs and available to send to the origin. Vercel provides request IDs and request logs; application correlation fields can be forwarded for origin work. A cached content reference must remain separate from the current request ID.
r31.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
 participant A as Request A
 participant C as CDN cache
 participant O as Content origin
 participant B as Request B
 participant L as Native request logs
 A->>C: Same content URL, first request
 C->>O: MISS, fetch content
 O-->>C: Content with fill reference
 C-->>A: New request identity, fill reference
 C-->>L: Record for A
 B->>C: Same URL, later request
 C-->>B: HIT, new request identity, same fill
 C-->>L: Record for B
r31.flow: Recorded relationship between successive requests and a shared content fill. The arrows describe the logical flow, not an internal platform trace.
r31.sectionTitle: Compare current request and cached fill
paragraphs: A fetched public content on a MISS. B requested the same URL and received a HIT: its native request ID changed, while the content fill ID stayed the same. One content-origin call was recorded for this path. Open R32 next to make the same comparison in a real browser and match each current request to its cookie log.
r31.detail: The full response x-vercel-id is retained separately from the native log requestId. Matching suffixes were observed, but parsing that format is not the correlation contract. R32 demonstrates an exact custom-emission envelope requestId join for its bounded case.
r31.decision: Agree the identifiers forwarded to the origin and stored by log consumers. Keep raw platform, application, parent and attempt IDs separate; do not rely on parsing an observed ID format.

r38.title: What must the replacement PIM processing do?
r38.note: The invocation rules are known; the real PIM program and functional contract are missing.
r38.intro: Akamai invokes the PIM EdgeWorker for selected requests, but the supplied rules do not contain the program itself. Routing Middleware is a candidate for request decisions; a Function can handle explicit origin-response processing. The real stages and response changes must be known before choosing the complete replacement.
r38.scope: Explanation of the known requirements. No real PIM implementation has been tested.
r38.diagram:
flowchart LR
 E[Eligibility and state rules] --> D[Stage design — unresolved]
 I[Required inputs and outputs] --> D
 S[Program source and dependencies] --> D
 C[Origin and cache interaction] --> D
 D --> G[Golden request and response cases]
r38.flow: These are inputs needed to define the replacement, not an assertion about where the missing program runs.
r38.sectionTitle: What is known, and what is missing
paragraphs: The rules identify cookie, path, method, retry, subrequest and waiting-room conditions. They identify invocation and status, not the operations PIM performs on a request or response.

The RP-status-only mock used in R39 records path, query and method, then returns a configured status. Its backend returns synthetic JSON. Neither that test nor the separate R40 child example proves customer body changes, per-visitor cached-body processing or cookie policy.
r38.detail: Routing Middleware runs before the cache; do not assume it supplies a general post-cache response-body hook. Before-origin, after-origin and cache-related stages must be recovered from the program or contract. The PIM name alone does not establish Akamai Page Integrity Manager.
r38.decision: Obtain the PIM source and dependencies, or a functional contract with stage order, request/response changes, external calls and golden inputs/outputs. Establish whether any processing must modify a cached body separately for each visitor.

r39.title: Can a failed request retry once without repeating processing?
r39.note: Custom browser retry and loop guard demonstrated. Confirm actual failure policy and whether literal query bytes matter.
r39.intro: The current failure rule returns a 302 to the same path with ewresponse=retry and x-ew-rp-error: true. In this custom Function example, the browser follows that redirect, and the retry marker skips the parent processing before the backend is called.
r39.scope: Live example on an owned test service · recorded fallback from 27 September 2026. The customer PIM program is not implemented.
r39.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
 participant B as Browser
 participant F as Custom Function
 participant P as Test processing
 participant O as Test backend
 B->>F: GET /checkout?cart=123
 F->>P: Run eligible parent processing
 P-->>F: Failure status
 F-->>B: 302 with error header and retry Location
 B->>F: GET /checkout?cart=123&ewresponse=retry
 Note over F: Marker present — skip parent processing
 F->>O: Fetch terminal response
 O-->>F: 200 or 503
 F-->>B: Terminal response without another redirect
r39.flow: The retry is another browser request. The Function does not fetch its own retry URL.
paragraphs: The marked request skips processing and calls the backend once. Query values and order survive; percent-escape case can change (%2f → %2F), so byte-identical preservation is not claimed.
r39.observation: The recorded browser runs returned 302 → 200 and 302 → 503, each with processing=1 and backend=1. A direct marked request returned 200 with processing=0 and backend=1. These are saved observations, not a new run.
r39.detail: Query values, duplicate-parameter order and empty values were retained. Percent-escape case normalized (%2f → %2F); literal query-byte identity is not demonstrated. Failure matching uses case-sensitive substring exclusions for success and unimplementedHandler, without trimming; confirm this with customer golden cases. Only GET enters the deployed retry branch. Counters are independent records from owned test endpoints, not native Log Drain records.
r39.decision: Confirm PIM failure statuses, terminal response policy and whether query strings must remain byte-identical. The bounded retry works; the full PIM program remains the separate R38 question.

r40.title: Can internal requests keep their parent identity without repeating processing?
r40.note: Custom parent/child correlation and recursion guard demonstrated. Real PIM routes, trust and log policy still need the contract.
r40.intro: The current rules mark PIM subrequests and distinguish them in logs. This owned Function example signs a child marker, keeps parent and child IDs together, and accepts only one child level. Two deliberate deliveries create one child event in the test ledger.
r40.scope: Live example on an owned test service · recorded fallback from 27 September 2026. The customer PIM program is not implemented.
r40.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
 participant P as Parent Function
 participant C as Child Function
 participant L as Test event ledger
 P->>C: Signed parent and child IDs, depth 1
 C->>L: Record child ID
 L-->>C: New event
 C-->>P: duplicate false
 P->>C: Same signed parent and child IDs
 C->>L: Record same child ID
 L-->>C: Existing event
 C-->>P: duplicate true
 Note over C: No further child request
r40.flow: These are server-to-server HTTP deliveries. The custom child handler stops recursion at depth 1; the ledger deduplicates only its event record.
paragraphs: The counters describe an owned event ledger. Deduplicating its child record does not prove exactly-once business execution or native Log Drain deduplication.
r40.observation: Recorded result: two HTTP deliveries, one parent and one unique child event. Event-ledger deduplication does not establish exactly-once business execution or native Log Drain deduplication.
r40.detail: Unsigned, tampered and expired markers returned 401; a signed depth of 2 returned 409. A public x-pim-ew header alone does not authorize the child endpoint.
r40.decision: Agree the real child routes, trusted-marker propagation, recursion rules and required log fields from the PIM contract. Define duplicate business-effect handling separately from this event ledger.

r36.title: Who is allowed through the waiting room?
r36.note: Admission requires an owned integration and policy; a holding page supplies only the response.
r36.intro: The current waiting room protects selected checkout and login requests, gives admitted visitors temporary access, and exposes waiting-room state to later processing. A dedicated integration or an explicitly designed admission service must supply that decision on Vercel.
r36.scope: Proposed integration flow. No complete waiting-room admission demonstration has been run.

r36.flow: Proposed flow only. The provider, capacity policy, visitor state and processing order still need to be selected and validated.
paragraphs: Serving a waiting page and deciding who can proceed are separate behaviors. The current configuration includes temporary privilege and waiting-room cookies, selected paths and method rules.
The replacement must preserve the intended admission, bypass and failure policy, then pass the correct state to subsequent processing. The R35 holding-page example does not make those decisions.
r36.observation: There is no verified queue, capacity or fairness behavior in the existing workshop packs.

r36.decision: Choose the active replacement product and owner, and agree capacity, fairness, bypass, failure behavior and queue-to-admission-to-processing order.

r01.note: Native domain mapping candidate; the authoritative host and environment inventory is still needed.

For each hostname, record whether it serves content, redirects, or belongs to a separate service. Add DNS and certificate owners, the target environment, and the replacement for the Akamai-specific staging address.

r02.title: Where should each service path go?
r02.intro: The current property names separate application and asset origins for services such as basket, checkout, search and product pages. Vercel external rewrites can forward selected paths to existing origins while keeping the visitor’s URL.
r02.note: External rewrites are a candidate; the complete ordered path-to-origin contract is missing.

  B --> C[Application origin]
  B --> D[Asset origin]

paragraphs: A route needs its match, destination host, forwarded Host, path-prefix change, query behavior and priority. An origin variable by itself does not establish which requests reach it.
Use specific service rules before the default destination. R19 illustrates conditional selection on owned test origins; it does not validate the customer’s basket, checkout or asset routes.
r02.decision: Obtain the ordered route matrix or raw rule export, then confirm the origin, Host, rewritten path and query for each service.
r02.detail: The diagram explains the proposed architecture rather than a captured request. Origin TLS policy remains R03.

r04.title: Which visitor IP should the origin trust?
r04.intro: The current rule removes an incoming True-Client-IP value and replaces it with the trusted visitor address. Proposed middleware would write that origin header from Vercel’s trusted request metadata, with an explicit policy for any CDN in front.
r04.note: Custom header mapping candidate; spoof resistance and a dual-CDN IP chain are unverified.
r04.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Visitor request] --> B[Vercel trusted IP metadata]
  B --> C[Replace True-Client-IP]
  C --> D[Origin request]
  E[Client-supplied True-Client-IP] -. ignored .-> C
r04.flow: Proposed direct-to-Vercel flow. If another proxy fronts Vercel, establish its trust contract before interpreting the address as the visitor IP.
paragraphs: Copying a client-supplied True-Client-IP would let a visitor choose the address the origin believes. The replacement must overwrite that value using the approved platform metadata.

Vercel documents that it overwrites forwarded IP values by default when behind another proxy. Its Enterprise Trusted Proxy option is a separate arrangement; simply preserving an incoming header does not establish a trustworthy chain.
r04.decision: Confirm whether requests arrive directly or through another CDN, then capture the forwarded header at an owned origin and verify that a spoofed incoming value cannot win.
r04.detail: Current request-header documentation was read on 27 September 2026. No dedicated end-to-end spoofing or dual-CDN test has been run for this page.

r18.title: How do flags and per-request values keep their order?
r18.intro: The current property initializes environment values and request flags, then changes some of them in later branches. The proposed Vercel design separates environment configuration from a fresh state object for every request, with Global Config available for operational toggles.
r18.note: Custom state model proposed; later overrides and evaluation order remain to recover.
r18.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Environment configuration] --> B[Fresh request state]
  C[Request inputs] --> B
  B --> D[Ordered conditions]
  D --> E[Final routing and log values]
r18.flow: Proposed state flow. Configuration is shared deliberately; mutable request state is created separately for each visitor.
paragraphs: The summary reports personalization on, the legacy feature flag off, Botify enabled and several blank or false runtime defaults. Those defaults do not prove which final values win after all conditions run.

Network labeling illustrates the ordering issue: it begins unknown and becomes production or staging under later conditions. The migration needs an explicit environment mapping rather than copying Akamai region labels.
r18.decision: Recover the request and response evaluation order, identify the final writer for each value, and agree which flags need runtime changes versus deployment configuration.
r18.detail: Official docs now call Edge Config “Global Config”; the proposed state design has not been validated against a complete customer trace.

r41.title: Who owns each redirect rule?
r41.intro: The customer asks whether redirects should live in one site-wide policy or in path-based groups. The proposed design keeps source rules grouped by owner and produces one deterministic order for evaluation.
r41.note: Governance proposal; rule volume, ownership and publishing workflow are undecided.
r41.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Team and path rule groups] --> B[Review overlaps and priority]
  B --> C[One published rule order]
  C --> D[Versioned change and rollback]
r41.flow: Proposed authoring and publishing model. Team grouping does not imply independently competing routing policies.
paragraphs: Path groups can make editing and accountability clear while a shared publishing step detects duplicate sources, loops and overlapping matches. Each rule should have an owner and an agreed priority.

Vercel offers configuration redirects and bulk redirect tooling. Bulk redirects target simple exact paths rather than wildcard or header matches, and run before deployment routes. Choose the authoring workflow and precedence after establishing the required rule types and volume.
r41.decision: Agree rule count, owning teams, approval and rollback requirements, then choose the redirect tooling and define how overlapping rules are resolved.
r41.detail: This is a design decision, not a demonstrated CDN parity result. No customer redirect rules have been published.

r42.title: Which rule wins when several conditions match?
r42.intro: The current property combines path, header, cookie, IP and flag conditions with later overrides and WAF-dependent decisions. Vercel matchers and custom logic provide building blocks, but the complete execution order must be translated explicitly.
r42.note: Ordinary predicates have candidate mappings; WAF-result timing and precedence remain unresolved.
r42.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Initialize request state] --> B[Evaluate available conditions]
  B --> C[Apply ordered overrides]
  C --> D[Choose response or destination]
  E[Required security result] -. availability unresolved .-> B
r42.flow: Logical translation model, not an asserted Vercel internal execution trace. Only values available at a given stage can influence that stage.
paragraphs: Path, header, cookie and query matches can use native conditions. Custom logic can express compound decisions, but percentage allocation belongs to the separate R17 audience policy.
A WAF result is an additional input with a timing dependency. The migration has not established that an equivalent security result is available before the delivery decision that consumes it.
r42.decision: Build the ordered request and response rule graph from the raw export, then confirm WAF-result availability and expected final values for overlapping matches.
r42.detail: Do not translate numeric Akamai WAF rule IDs into assumed Vercel equivalents. The security-result contract remains with the security owners.

r11.title: How should CONSENTMGR change consent and cookies?
r11.intro: The current CONSENTMGR branch reads legacy consent categories only when its feature flag is on, then clears selected experiment cookies on decline. The proposed Vercel mapping is a custom parser and ordered decision table using request and response cookie APIs.
r11.note: Custom parser proposed; the active flag branch and exact encoded/legacy grammar need confirmation.
r11.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Request cookies] --> B{Legacy branch enabled?}
  B -->|No| C[Keep initial consent state]
  B -->|Yes| D[Parse CONSENTMGR]
  D --> E[Apply category decisions]
  E --> F[Expire affected cookies]
r11.flow: Proposed translation of this consent source only. R12 covers OptanonConsent and the unresolved precedence when both sources exist.
paragraphs: The initial state accepts necessary cookies and declines functional, performance and marketing categories. In the enabled branch, c7 controls functional, c1 performance and c3 marketing; plain and encoded markers and older consent:true forms appear in the summary.

Functional decline expires the PDP experiment cookie. Marketing decline expires the content and audience experiment cookies. These changes need the original cookie scope and the rule’s actual parsing order.
r11.decision: Confirm whether this flag-gated branch is active, recover its exact legacy and encoded parsing rules, and agree precedence with OptanonConsent before implementing the parser.
r11.detail: The reported feature flag defaults off. This is an explanation of a custom implementation candidate, not a tested consent integration.

r12.title: How should OptanonConsent groups affect the request?
r12.intro: The current OptanonConsent branch extracts its groups field and applies category decisions, including cookie expiry on decline. The proposed implementation shares a consent state model with R11 while retaining this source’s own parsing and gating rules.
r12.note: Custom parser proposed; consent-source precedence and the missing V2STACK condition remain open.
r12.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[OptanonConsent cookie] --> B[Extract groups field]
  B --> C{Group 1 accepted?}
  C -->|Yes| D[Evaluate category groups]
  C -->|No| E[Keep applicable prior state]
  D --> F[Update consent and cookie expiry]
r12.flow: Proposed translation of the summarized branches. The prior state depends on the unresolved ordering of both consent sources.
paragraphs: Group 1 acceptance gates the individual category branches. Group 3 controls functional, group 2 performance and group 4 marketing; the performance branch also refers to a V2STACK condition absent from the supplied expression detail.
The all-accepted pattern requires groups 1, 2, 3 and 4. Encoded and plain markers are described, and declines clear the same category-related experiment cookies as the legacy branch.
r12.decision: Obtain the exact V2STACK expression and resolve which source wins when both consent cookies are present or conflict.
r12.detail: No deployed parser or golden-input consent test is claimed.

r13.title: Can each visitor receive only their own cookie changes?
r13.intro: The current rules set, update and expire browser cookies, and some also change the Cookie header sent to the origin. The proposed Vercel implementation handles those two directions separately and verifies that shared cached content cannot carry another visitor’s cookie changes.
r13.note: Cookie APIs provide a candidate; response Set-Cookie isolation on cache HIT and MISS is unverified.
r13.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant L as Per-request cookie logic
  participant C as Content path and cache
  B->>L: Current request cookies
  L->>C: Deliberately updated request Cookie
  C-->>L: Content response
  L-->>B: Visitor-specific Set-Cookie changes
r13.flow: Proposed logical behavior, not a captured cache pipeline. Request Cookie mutation and response Set-Cookie are separate operations.
r13.sectionTitle: Separate content sharing from cookie changes
paragraphs: Updating the upstream Cookie header affects the current origin request. Returning Set-Cookie asks the browser to change subsequent requests; one does not automatically prove the other.

R32 shows each browser request logging its current cookie, and R24 shows bounded public cache variants. Neither demonstrates newly issued response cookies remaining isolated between visitors on both a MISS and a HIT.
r13.decision: Agree each cookie’s scope and mutation rules, then verify new, changed and expired response cookies across two visitors and cache HIT/MISS without losing the required upstream mutation.
r13.detail: The source’s Set-Cookie pass policy needs translation at the selected cache layer. No response-cookie isolation proof is asserted.

r14.title: How do affiliate and loyalty links become cookies?
r14.intro: The current rules copy cjevent and loyaltysignal query values into cookies with the same names. The proposed Vercel middleware extracts those values and sets response cookies using the agreed encoding, attributes and consent conditions.
r14.note: Custom extraction candidate; encoding, duplicate parameters, attributes and effective consent gates remain to confirm.
r14.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Affiliate or loyalty query value] --> B[Extract using agreed rules]
  B --> C[Apply effective consent condition]
  C --> D[Set corresponding response cookie]
r14.flow: Proposed mapping. The consent condition must be recovered from the effective source rules; this page does not invent a new gate.
paragraphs: The summary specifies path /, the default domain, Secure enabled, HttpOnly disabled and a 395-day expiry. It does not fully establish the domain, SameSite or encoding contract.
Repeated parameters, empty values and percent-encoded characters need explicit expected outcomes. A generic URL parser’s choice should not silently become the customer policy.
r14.decision: Confirm the effective consent gates, duplicate-value and encoding behavior, and complete cookie attributes before implementing the two query-to-cookie rules.
r14.detail: No dedicated browser test has been run. The declared expiry is a requested cookie attribute, not proof that every browser will retain it for that period.

r15.title: What decides the analytics channel cookie?
r15.intro: The current rule creates analytics_channel when absent, defaults it to ecomm and changes it to mcomm using physical device dimensions. Cookie creation has a Vercel implementation path; an equivalent source for that physical-size decision is unresolved.
r15.note: Cookie mechanics are a candidate; equivalent physical-device input is missing.
r15.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A{Cookie already present?} -->|Yes| B[Retain existing value]
  A -->|No| C[Start with ecomm]
  C --> D{Physical size condition?}
  D -->|Matches| E[Use mcomm]
  D -->|Does not match| F[Use ecomm]
  E --> G[Response and upstream Cookie]
  F --> G
r15.flow: Current decision as summarized. The physical-size input in the proposed replacement has not been established.
paragraphs: The source uses physical height at most 145 and width at most 80, without specifying units. It writes the selected value both to the response and to the outgoing Cookie header, with path / and an expiry of 31 December 2038.
Browser viewport or screen resolution does not establish those physical dimensions. A user-agent mobile label from R16 is also a different input; substituting it requires an explicit policy decision.
r15.decision: Identify the physical-size data source and units, or agree a revised classification rule, then confirm persistence and both cookie directions.
r15.detail: The physical-size branch is a requirement fact, not a Vercel device-metadata capability claim.

r16.title: Which requests should count as mobile?
r16.intro: The current property marks a request mobile when its device profile says so or an is_mobile request header is true. A proposed Vercel implementation can use user-agent classification plus an explicitly trusted signal, but the customer’s device profile equivalence is not established.
r16.note: Classification candidate; device matrix, header trust and redirect policies are unresolved.
r16.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[User-agent classification] --> C[Agreed mobile decision]
  B[Approved trusted signal] --> C
  C --> D[Request state]
  D --> E[Origin header and dependent rules]
r16.flow: Proposed inputs. Trusting a signal must be a deliberate policy; accepting an arbitrary client header is not shown as verified.
paragraphs: The current rule sets request state and the outgoing is_mobile=true header. The overview additionally asks about device-dependent redirects, but their detailed rules are absent.

Next.js provides a user-agent parser with a device type. That is a useful candidate input, but a parser result alone does not prove parity with Akamai Device_Profile or the physical-size decision in R15.
r16.decision: Agree the device matrix, unknown-device behavior, trusted-header policy and any device redirect rules, then compare classifications against representative requests.
r16.detail: No customer device classification matrix has been tested.

r17.title: How does a visitor keep the same experiment group?
r17.intro: The current source names audience buckets for search, product, browse and content, but omits the allocation policy. Stable custom assignment with shared configuration and consent-aware persistence is a candidate; the workshop’s cache variants do not supply that policy.
r17.note: Assignment design remains unresolved; bucket names do not establish allocation or persistence.
r17.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Consent and eligibility] --> B{Valid existing assignment?}
  B -->|Yes| C[Reuse group]
  B -->|No| D[Apply agreed allocation]
  D --> E[Persist under agreed policy]
  C --> F[Select content variant]
  E --> F
r17.flow: Proposed assignment design. Weights, eligibility, stable identity and reassignment are customer decisions, not implemented defaults.
paragraphs: Numbered bucket constants and a Bot bucket describe possible values, not traffic percentages or how a visitor receives one. Consent declines also clear some experiment cookies, which may affect later assignment.
R24 demonstrates sharing content within an already chosen public cohort and separating different cohorts. It does not demonstrate production allocation, consent, persistence or reassignment.
r17.decision: Obtain the actual audience policy: weights, eligibility and bot exclusions, identity, persistence, consent behavior and reassignment rules.
r17.detail: Global Config can hold allocation data; it does not infer the missing allocation algorithm. Rolling Releases is not assumed to be an equivalent policy.

r25.title: Can related pages be purged together?
r25.intro: The current consent branches append a cookie-list cache tag while keeping existing tags. Vercel cache tags provide a candidate for grouping cached responses and purging that group, with an explicit choice between background invalidation and foreground refresh.
r25.note: Native tags are a candidate; attachment across both consent branches and purge semantics need validation.
r25.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Cookie-list response] --> B[Keep existing tags and append group tag]
  B --> C[Cached tagged content]
  D[Chosen purge operation] --> C
  C --> E[Next request refreshes under chosen policy]
r25.flow: Proposed tag lifecycle. Tagging for purge is separate from R26 reporting and billing attribution.
paragraphs: The source appends an environment-and-brand cookie-list tag on /help/cookie-list* inside either consent branch. The migration needs to retain the existing tags as well as the added group tag.
Vercel invalidation can serve stale content while refreshing in the background. Deletion makes the next request wait for regenerated content. Choose the behavior required by the content change.
r25.decision: Confirm the desired purge semantics, then verify tag attachment and preservation through both consent branches and the resulting refresh behavior.
r25.detail: Official docs describe Vercel-Cache-Tag for Function and external-rewrite responses. No dedicated customer tag/purge test has been performed.

r30.title: Which compression and resource hints must remain?
r30.intro: The current property enables Brotli, including for non-cacheable content, and contains conditional resource-hint settings with later overrides. Vercel supports CDN compression; resource hints need an explicit application design based on the rules that are actually active.
r30.note: Compression has a native mapping; active learned-hint behavior and branch semantics remain unverified.
r30.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Response content] --> B[Negotiated CDN compression]
  B --> C[Browser response]
  D[Effective resource-hint policy] --> E[Application headers or markup]
  E --> C
r30.flow: Two separate proposed concerns: transfer encoding and resource discovery. Compression does not establish adaptive-hint equivalence.
paragraphs: The source sets the resource optimizer on and later off. Push, preconnect and font preload appear enabled in one branch and disabled in a WAF-triggered branch; experiment mode is reported off.

The useful observation for compression is the actual Content-Encoding on representative cached and uncached responses. For hints, first identify the active behavior and its consumer before choosing explicit headers or markup.
r30.decision: Confirm which adaptive hints are active and valuable, then validate compression on the required response types and agree the application-owned replacement for those hints.
r30.detail: Current compression docs describe Brotli and gzip negotiation. This page makes no claim of automatic learned resource-hint or HTTP push parity.

r03.scope: Recorded hosted evidence · 24 September 2026. The temporary origin/tunnel has not been restored or tested for this page; these are saved observations.
r03.title: Can the origin use the required Host, SNI and certificate policy?
r03.note: Owned custom TLS controls passed; the native route did not reject the tested mismatched certificate.
r03.intro: The current origin policy distinguishes destination, HTTP Host, TLS server name and trusted certificates. An owned Node.js proxy demonstrated separate controls for those values. The tested native forwarding path did not meet the expected certificate rejection.
r03.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
 participant C as Client
 participant F as Custom proxy Function
 participant O as Owned TLS origin
 C->>F: Request an approved test case
 F->>O: Connect to destination with selected SNI and CA trust
 alt Certificate accepted
 F->>O: HTTP request with independently selected Host
 O-->>F: Origin response
 F-->>C: 200 with recorded TLS facts
 else Wrong name or untrusted CA
 F-->>C: 502 before origin HTTP response
 end
r03.flow: Custom proxy path only. The native forwarding comparison below is a separate test. Visitor TLS is the separate R10 connection.
paragraphs: With the dedicated test CA and correct name, the origin reported SNI origin-a.workshop.test and HTTP Host app-b.workshop.test. Changing the name or removing that CA trust caused the custom path to fail before an origin HTTP response.

rows: Native forwarding: private CA + mismatched name

r03.observation: The native certificate mismatch is part of the result; the successful custom controls do not resolve it.
r03.detail: Owned hostname and resolved IPv4 controls, separate Host and SNI choices, and recovery were tested. This does not establish customer private-origin access, complete trust policy or retries. The recorded dependency was a Mac origin and a temporary raw TCP tunnel.
r03.decision: Confirm the required destination, Host, SNI and CA/name policy, then choose a supported native or custom architecture and validate retries and origin access.

r28.scope: Recorded hosted evidence · 24 September 2026. The temporary origin/tunnel has not been restored or tested for this page; these are saved observations.
r28.title: Does content arrive incrementally, and does cancellation reach the origin?
r28.note: Incremental chunks and bounded cancellation passed; full transport controls and lifetime remain open.
r28.intro: The current delivery settings cover streaming and transport behavior. The custom proxy streamed an owned origin response incrementally and passed a client abort signal upstream. This tests two observable outcomes, not every HTTP-version or buffering control.
r28.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
 participant B as Client
 participant F as Custom proxy
 participant O as Streaming origin
 B->>F: Request stream
 F->>O: Request with client abort signal
 loop Until completion or cancellation
 O-->>F: Next chunk
 F-->>B: Forward chunk
 end
 B->>F: Abort request in separate cancellation test
 F->>O: Abort upstream work
 Note over O: Stop observed after in-flight chunks
r28.flow: Logical streaming path. The complete eight-chunk stream and the 40-chunk cancellation case are separate recorded tests.
r28.sectionTitle: Read the recorded arrival and cancellation results
paragraphs: In the eight-chunk test, the first chunk arrived before the origin finished. In the separate cancellation case, the client stopped after two chunks; the origin stopped after six of forty with completed=false. Cancellation was not instantaneous.

rows: First arrival 1,966 ms; last arrival 4,065 ms

r28.detail: The recorded Node 24 Function used maxDuration=60 and supportsCancellation=true. Local origin, direct tunnel and deployed controls separated cadence from proxy buffering. A 30-second idle/recovery check is not a long-lived stream guarantee.
r28.decision: Specify required HTTP versions, buffering/backpressure behavior and maximum lifetime, then validate those controls with a durable origin and representative traffic.

r27.scope: Recorded hosted evidence · 24 September 2026. The temporary origin/tunnel has not been restored or tested for this page; these are saved observations.
r27.title: Can the chat connection survive through the proposed relay?
r27.statusText: Custom relay demonstrated; duration test failed
r27.note: Two-connection relay passed bounded message tests; native passthrough and platform cutoff remain unresolved.
r27.intro: The existing chat uses WebSockets, but its upstream topology and session contract are missing. The recorded custom Function relay connected the browser to an owned external backend using two separate sockets. It is an architectural alternative that still needs the chat requirements.
r27.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
 participant B as Browser
 participant R as Custom relay
 participant O as Owned WebSocket backend
 B->>R: Authenticated upgrade and subprotocol
 R->>O: Separate authenticated WebSocket connection
 O-->>R: Upstream connection ID
 R-->>B: Relay ID and upstream ID
 B->>R: Text or binary message
 R->>O: Forward message
 O-->>R: Echo
 R-->>B: Forward echo
 Note over B,O: Reconnect creates new connections, no hidden replay
r27.flow: Two connections with application-managed forwarding and closure. This is not a transparent native passthrough demonstration.
paragraphs: Real Chrome sent unchanged text and binary bytes through the relay and negotiated the test subprotocol. The direct upstream control worked; the native rewrite probe did not complete the browser WebSocket upgrade.

rows: Code 4000 at the configured 25-second application timer; reconnect created new IDs
FAILED expectation: still open at the 43-second safety ceiling

r27.observation: 18 of 19 recorded checks passed. The platform cutoff remains unverified; the application timer is not evidence of the platform limit.
r27.detail: Recorded controls also covered upstream close, unavailable-upstream recovery and 20-second idle. No production load, durable session restoration or customer authentication topology was validated. The relay ran on the then-tested Functions WebSocket beta with Node v24.20.0 and Fluid compute.
r27.decision: Obtain the chat topology, authentication, lifetime and recovery contract; agree whether a two-socket relay is acceptable and resolve the platform-duration behavior before committing to it.

r10.title: Can the response report the visitor’s actual TLS version and cipher?
r10.statusText: Trustworthy exact pair unmet in test
r10.note: The tested Function interface did not expose an authoritative negotiated visitor TLS pair.
r10.intro: The current policy returns diagnostic headers for the visitor’s negotiated TLS version and cipher. In the tested Vercel interface, Function socket data did not provide that pair, and caller-supplied lookalike headers were untrusted. Origin TLS data answers a different question.
r10.scope: Recorded hosted observation · 24 September 2026. No replacement metadata source has been validated.
r10.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
 participant C as TLS test client
 participant V as Vercel HTTPS entry
 participant F as Probe Function
 C->>V: Negotiate visitor TLS connection
 Note over C,V: Client records actual version and cipher
 V->>F: Forward HTTP request
 F->>F: Inspect available socket and headers
 F-->>C: No trustworthy exact visitor pair established
r10.flow: The TLS client connects to Vercel. No external-origin TLS connection is present in this test.
r10.sectionTitle: Compare client truth with Function-visible data
paragraphs: Strict certificate-verified client connections recorded their negotiated version and cipher. The Function socket was plaintext and had no getProtocol/getCipher methods; HTTPS and fingerprint signals did not establish the exact negotiated pair.
r10.observation: In forged-header controls, Akamai-TLS and Akamai-CIPHER contained the caller’s FORGED values. Echoing those headers would not provide trustworthy diagnostics.
r10.detail: This is a scoped test result, not a claim that no Vercel product or future interface can ever expose the metadata. A replacement needs an authoritative source available when constructing the required response.
r10.decision: Establish the supported metadata source and its trust boundary, or agree to retire these exact diagnostic headers.
